nameStory: The 'godwit' part of this bird's name comes from its distinctive call, which early English speakers thought sounded like 'god-wit!' The 'Hudsonian' refers to Hudson Bay in Canada, where many of these birds pass through during their epic migrations between the Arctic and South America.
description: The Hudsonian Godwit is a large, elegant shorebird with an impressively long, slightly upturned bill perfect for probing deep into mud and sand. These long-legged waders are about the size of a small duck, with a sleek body built for incredibly long-distance travel. In breeding plumage, they sport rich rusty-red underparts that fade to gray and white in winter, while their backs remain mottled brown and black year-round. They're remarkable marathon fliers, traveling from Arctic Canada all the way to Argentina twice each year.

idTips.label: Long upturned bill
idTips.description: The bill is noticeably long and curves slightly upward at the tip, perfect for reaching deep into soft mud - much longer than your thumb

idTips.label: Rusty breeding plumage
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, the neck and belly glow with deep brick-red or cinnamon coloring that's unmistakable among shorebirds

idTips.label: White wing stripe
idTips.description: In flight, look for a bold white stripe running down the length of each dark wing - very prominent against the darker flight feathers

idTips.label: Long dark legs
idTips.description: Legs extend well beyond the tail in flight and are proportionally longer than most sandpipers, colored dark gray to black

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than most sandpipers with an upright, elegant posture when feeding - about the size of a small duck

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Probes deeply into mud with rhythmic up-and-down motions, often submerging the entire bill and even part of the head

habitat: Look for Hudsonian Godwits along New England's coastal mudflats, salt marshes, and shallow tidal pools during migration periods. They prefer soft, muddy shorelines where they can easily probe for marine worms and small shellfish. Occasionally found at inland freshwater locations like flooded fields or large pond edges, but coastal areas are your best bet.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration through New England occurs in May, when birds show their spectacular rusty-red breeding plumage and are most easily identified.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in summer as most birds are far north in Arctic Canada breeding grounds. Any sightings would likely be non-breeding individuals.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration brings birds back through in August and September, but they're in duller gray and white winter plumage, making identification more challenging.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter as virtually all birds have continued south to South America. Any winter sightings would be exceptional.

funFact: Hudsonian Godwits make one of the most incredible non-stop flights in the bird world - some fly directly from Canada to South America in a single 4,000-mile journey over the Atlantic Ocean, flying continuously for 6 days and nights without landing!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Marbled Godwits, but Hudsonian Godwits have a white wing stripe (Marbled Godwits show cinnamon wing linings) and darker legs. Memory trick: 'Hudsonian has the Highway' - think of that white wing stripe as a highway stripe down the wing.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'Hudsonian,' these birds don't actually breed around Hudson Bay itself, but rather in more remote Arctic regions of Canada and Alaska. The name stuck from early observations of migrating birds in the Hudson Bay area.
compareHints: Compared to the Marbled Godwit (the other godwit regularly seen in New England), Hudsonian Godwits are smaller with a straighter bill and completely different wing pattern in flight. Bar-tailed and Black-tailed Godwits are extremely rare vagrants in New England, but both lack the Hudsonian's distinctive white wing stripe and have different leg colors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the godwits, Marbled Godwits are the largest and show the most consistent warm brown coloration throughout the year.
Compared to the Hudsonian Godwit (the most similar species), bar-tailed godwits have that distinctive upturned bill and lack the bold white wing patches.
Among the godwits, Black-tailed is the only one with that distinctive white wingbar and the black-on-white tail pattern.
